## 1 Introduction

A large portion of the existing literature on nonlinear control comprises model-based approaches (e.g., backstepping, feedback linearization [1]) that depend on the availability of a sufficiently accurate analytical model of the system or plant to be controlled. There is an inherent assumption that such an analytic model can be obtained from the fundamental laws governing the system. However, there are many instances where a reliable and/or accurate analytical model of the system cannot be obtained in practice. Robust control theory can also be used to design a stabilizing controller for a nonlinear system under the assumption that at least a nominal realization of the system, either linear time-invariant (LTI) or linear time-varying (LTV), can be obtained (see, e.g., [2, 3, 4, Chapter 9]). In this setting, the system is described in linear fractional transformation (LFT) form, where the nominal system is connected in feedback with a 'perturbation' that captures all aspects of the system that do not fit within an LTI or LTV framework (e.g., nonlinearity, uncertainty, time delays). The control synthesis is then based on the input-output (I/O) properties of the perturbation, which are assumed to hold for some known structure and/or set of perturbations (e.g., integral quadratic constraints [5], structured singular value [6]). For a complex system, however, it is not trivial to quantify these I/O properties and ascertain if the accompanying assumptions hold, especially when the analytical form of the perturbation is not explicitly known.

Data-driven techniques are now becoming increasingly popular to overcome these issues [7]. For example, strategies are being proposed for determining I/O properties from sampled data (like dissipation inequalities [8] and passivity [9]). Also, data-driven approaches for robust control, with a focus on perturbations representing parametric uncertainties and unknown nonlinearity driven by states and/or parameters, are gaining popularity [10, 11, 12]. However, the class of perturbations for which the unknown nonlinearity is a function of both the states and control inputs is relatively less studied. Existing data-driven methods for this class of perturbations are either guaranteed to work in a small neighborhood of the equilibrium [13] or require extensive tuning of the associated control parameters to satisfy the underlying assumptions [14]. In light of these challenges associated with purely data-driven control, we have adopted an approach where I/O properties of the perturbation are established through data and subsequently used for control synthesis.

We consider a general nonlinear system and partition it into an LFT form, where the nominal system captures the system's LTI dynamics about an equilibrium and the perturbation comprises higher-order nonlinearities, which are functions of both the states and control inputs and are not necessarily known analytically. Assuming I/O samples of the perturbation are available, local norm bounds are derived. A robust state-feedback controller is synthesized that asymptotically stabilizes the nonlinear system locally within the sampled region for all perturbations satisfying the norm bounds. Since the norm bounds, which depend on control inputs, are used in the synthesis, the synthesized controller must ensure that the control inputs remain within the sampling set. Moreover, the main synthesis problem involves non-convex constraints. We relax the main problem into three semi-definite programs (SDPs) that are solved iteratively. To summarize, the contribution of this work is an iterative control synthesis method that results in local asymptotic stabilization of a nonlinear system, where the system's nonlinearities are analytically unknown, but available through sampling, and depend explicitly on control inputs.

The function $\hat{\phi}(x^{k})$ represents the update rule of $\mathbf{w}^{k}$, with $\mathbf{w}^{k} = \left( w_{1}^{k}, \ldots, w_{n}^{k} \right)$.

The $\mathbf{w}^{k}$ is updated by Algorithm 1, which takes $\mathbf{w}^{k} = \left( w_{1}^{k}, \ldots, w_{n}^{k} \right)$ as input, and outputs a result $\mathbf{w}^{k+1}$.

The $\mathbf{w}^{k+1}$ is defined as follows:

$$
\mathbf{w}^{k+1} = \Phi (\mathbf{w}^{k}, \mathbf{x}).
$$

The function $\Phi$ is an update function that maps $\mathbf{w}^{k}$, $\mathbf{x}$, and possibly other parameters to $\mathbf{w}^{k+1}$.

The $\Phi$ is defined as follows:

$$
\Phi (\mathbf{w}^{k}, \mathbf{x}) = \mu \mathbf{w}^{k} + (1-\mu) \mathbf{w}^{k+1},
$$

where $\mu$ is a parameter that controls the update rate.

The update rate $\mu$ is a step size that determines how much the algorithm is updated in each iteration.

The $\mu$ is varied during training to control the learning rate, allowing the algorithm to adapt to different datasets and tasks.

Specifically, if $\mu$ is small, the algorithm updates slowly, and if $\mu$ is large, the algorithm updates quickly. This trade-off is known as the learning rate.

Extracting and reading KD triplets [34, 35, 36] from the encoded KD vector is straightforward (see Fig. 4), provided that the KD triplet is carefully constructed. While the causal KD triplet satisfies these properties, the non-causally used triplet is typically infeasible to directly use in control. Therefore, we propose a two-step procedure to create KD vectors consisting of inaccessible KD triplets. Although the resulting KD triplets contained in the KD vector represent not so easily accessible data for control, the two-step procedure enables sample-efficient algorithm for collecting KD triplets for the underlying continuous control task. The main contribution of our work is to provide an algorithmic framework that facilitates the generation and extraction of the accessible KD triplets which cannot be directly used for certain control tasks with existing KD algorithms.

## III CONTROL SYMETHIS

This section describes the synthesis of a static state-feedback controller \(\mathbf{K}\), which requires breaking the main synthesis problem into different sub-problems and iterating over these sub-problems to obtain a controller that is certified to render the closed-loop system (4) asymptotically stable within \(\mathbb{X}_{c}\). We will start by specifying structures of the sets \(\mathbb{X}_{c}\) and \(\mathbb{U}_{c}\) that will be used in the remainder of the letter. The local region \(\mathbb{X}_{c}\) is taken to be a family of ellipsoids parameterized by \(\mathbf{W}>0\), i.e., \(\mathbb{X}_{c}=\mathcal{E}_{n_{x}}(\mathbf{W})\), where \(\mathbf{W}\) is chosen appropriately such that \(\mathbb{X}_{c}\subseteq\mathbb{X}\). Similarly, we take \(\mathbb{U}_{c}=r\mathcal{B}_{n_{u}}\), where \(r>0\) is the parameter related to the control input magnitude and is chosen such that \(\mathbb{U}_{c}\subseteq\mathbb{U}\). With these sets defined, the main synthesis problem is summarized in the next result.

**Theorem III.1**: _Let \(\mathbf{W}>0\) and \(r>0\) be chosen such that \(\mathbb{X}_{c}=\mathcal{E}_{n_{x}}(\mathbf{W})\subseteq\mathbb{X}\) and \(\mathbb{U}_{c}=r\mathcal{B}_{n_{u}}\subseteq\mathbb{U}\), respectively. Suppose Assumption II.2 holds with \(\mathbb{D}=\mathbb{X}_{c}\times\mathbb{U}_{c}\). Then, the closed-loop system (4) is locally asymptotically stable in \(\mathbb{X}_{c}\) for all \(\Delta_{i}\in\Delta_{\mathbb{D}_{i}}\), \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\), if there exist \(\mathbf{P}>0\), \(\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}\times n_{x}}\), \(\tau>0\), and \(\lambda_{i}>0\), \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\), such that_

\[\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})+(\mathbf{A}+ \mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\mathbf{P}\mathbf{B}_{2}& \Theta\\ \mathbf{B}_{2}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\boldsymbol{\Lambda}&{\bf 0}\\ \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\operatorname{T}}&{\bf 0}&\Xi\end{bmatrix}<0,\] (7)\[\begin{bmatrix}\tau^{2}\mathbf{I}&\mathbf{K}\\ \mathbf{K}^{\operatorname{T}}&\mathbf{W}^{-1}\mathbf{W}^{-1}\end{bmatrix}\geq 0,\] (8) \[\tau\leq r,\] (9)

_where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=-{\text{diag}}\left(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n_{w}}\right)\), and_

\[\Xi=-{\text{diag}}(\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\gamma_{1}^{2}}\mathbf{I},\dots,\frac{ \lambda_{n_{w}}}{\gamma_{n_{w}}^{2}}\mathbf{I}),\ \boldsymbol{\Theta}=\left[ \lambda_{1}\Phi_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n}\Phi_{n_{w}}\right],\] (10)

_with \(\Phi_{i}=\mathbf{C}_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}+\mathbf{K}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf {D}_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}\), \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\)._

_Proof:_  We establish the proof in three parts: first, we derive a condition that ensures asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system within the local region \(\mathbb{X}_{c}\) under the assumption that \(\delta{\bf u}=\mathbf{K}\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{U}_{c}\) for all \(\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}\); then, we obtain the equivalent stability condition (7); finally, we constrain the control signal such that \(\delta{\bf u}=\mathbf{K}\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{U}_{c}\) for all \(\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}\), which leads to (8) and (9).

_Part-1:_  Define the candidate Lyapunov function \(V=\delta{\bf x}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}\delta{\bf x}\) with \(\mathbf{P}>0\). Taking the time-derivative of \(V\) and using (4) results in

\[V=\delta{\bf x}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}\delta\dot{\bf x}+\delta\dot{\bf x }^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}\delta{\bf x}\]

\[=\begin{bmatrix}\delta{\bf x}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}^{\operatorname{T}}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{A}+ \mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})+(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})^{\operatorname {T}}\mathbf{P}&\mathbf{P}\mathbf{B}_{2}\\ \mathbf{B}_{2}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&{\bf 0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix }\delta{\bf x}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}.\]

The inputs and outputs of each \(\Delta_{i}\) can be rewritten using (4) as

\[\begin{bmatrix}{\bf v}_{i}\\ w_{i}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}(\mathbf{C}_{i}+\mathbf{D}_{i}\mathbf{K})& \mathbf{0}\\ \bf 0&\bf I_{n_{w}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta{\bf x}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}.\] (11)

Now, suppose \(\delta{\bf u}=\mathbf{K}\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{U}_{c}\) holds for all \(\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}\). Then, under Assumption II.2 with \(\mathbb{D}=\mathbb{X}_{c}\times\mathbb{U}_{c}\), we have \(w_{i}^{2}\leq\gamma_{i}^{2}\left\|{\bf v}_{i}\right\|^{2}\) for each \(\Delta_{i}\in\Delta_{\mathbb{D}_{i}}\), \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\), and for all \(\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}\), which is equivalently given by

\[\begin{bmatrix}{\bf v}_{i}\\ w_{i}\end{bmatrix}^{\operatorname{T}}\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_{i}^{2}\mathbf{I}& {\bf 0}\\ \bf 0&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{\bf v}_{i}\\ w_{i}\end{bmatrix}\geq 0.\] (12)

This, along with (11), leads to a quadratic constraint (QC) in \(\delta{\bf x}\) and \(\mathbf{w}\) for each \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\), expressed as

\[\begin{bmatrix}\delta{\bf x}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}^{\operatorname{T}}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_{i }^{2}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}&{\bf 0}\\ \bf 0&-1_{n_{w}}\bf I_{n_{w}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta{\bf x}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}}_{{\bf B}_{2}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}}\geq 0,\] (13)

where \(\Phi_{i}=\mathbf{C}_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}+\mathbf{K}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf {D}_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}\). In the current setting, all QCs of the form (13) for \(\Delta_{i}\in\Delta_{\mathbb{D}_{i}}\), \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\) hold for all \(\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}\). This would imply, through the S-procedure, that \(V<0\) for all \(\delta{\bf x}\in\mathbb{X}_{c}\) if there exists \(\lambda_{i}\geq 0,\ i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\) such that

\[\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})+ (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\mathbf {P}\mathbf{B}_{2}\\ \mathbf{B}_{2}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\bf 0\end{bmatrix}\] \[+\sum_{i=1}^{n_{w}}\lambda_{i}\begin{bmatrix}\gamma_{i}^{2}\Phi_{ i}\Phi_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}&{\bf 0}\\ \bf 0&-1_{n_{w}}\bf I_{n_{w}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\delta{\bf x}\\ \mathbf{w}\end{bmatrix}<0.\] (14)

This concludes the first part of the proof where we have derived a condition for local asymptotic stability.

_Part-2:_ Making the restriction that \(\lambda_{i}>0\) for all \(i\in\mathcal{N}_{n_{w}}\), allows for (14) to be rewritten as

\[\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})+ (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\mathbf {P}\mathbf{B}_{2}\\ \mathbf{B}_{2}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\end{bmatrix}\] \[-\sum_{i=1}^{n_{w}}\begin{bmatrix}-\lambda_{i}\Phi_{i}\frac{ \gamma_{i}^{2}}{\lambda_{i}}\Phi_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}\lambda_{i}&{\bf 0}\\ \bf 0&0\end{bmatrix}<0,\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=-\sum_{i=1}^{n_{w}}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{1}_{n_{w}}\mathbf{ 1}_{n_{w}}^{\operatorname{T}}=-{\text{diag}}\left(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n _{w}}\right)\). Each matrix in the sum above can be expressed as

\[{\begin{bmatrix}-\lambda_{i}\Phi_{i}\frac{\gamma_{i}^{2}}{\lambda_{i}}\Phi_{i} ^{\operatorname{T}}\lambda_{i}&{\bf 0}\\ {\bf 0}&0\end{bmatrix}}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{i}\Phi_{i}\\ \bf 0\end{bmatrix}\left(-\frac{\gamma_{i}^{2}}{\lambda_{i}}\mathbf{I}\right) \begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}\Phi_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}&{\bf 0}\\ \bf 0\end{bmatrix},\]

which leads to

\[\sum_{i=1}^{n_{w}}\begin{bmatrix}-\lambda_{i}\Phi_{i}\frac{\gamma_{i}^{2}}{ \lambda_{i}}\Phi_{i}^{\operatorname{T}}\lambda_{i}&{\bf 0}\\ {\bf 0}&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\Theta\\ \bf 0\end{bmatrix}({\Xi})^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\Theta\\ \bf 0\end{bmatrix}^{\operatorname{T}},\] (16)

where \(\Xi\) and \(\Theta\) are as shown in (10). Thus, (15) becomes

\[\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})+ (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}_{1}\mathbf{K})^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\mathbf {P}\mathbf{B}_{2}\\ \mathbf{B}_{2}^{\operatorname{T}}\mathbf{P}&\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\end{bmatrix}\] \[-\begin{bmatrix}\Theta\\ \bf 0\end{bmatrix}(\Xi)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\Theta\\ \bf 0\end{bmatrix}^{\operatorname{T}}<0.\]

Applying the Schur complement to (17) leads to (7), which completes the proof for the equivalent stability condition.

Example-2: Consider the inverted pendulum example in [13, Section V.B] in continuous time with the same unstable equilibrium at \((\mathbf{x}_{0},u_{0})=(\mathbf{0},0),\) which corresponds to the pendulum in upright position. The governing system is expressed in the closed-loop form as

\[\begin{split}\delta\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\left(\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ g&-1\end{bmatrix}+\mathbf{1}_{2_{2}}\mathbf{K}\right)\delta\mathbf{x}+\begin{ bmatrix}0\\ \tfrac{1}{l}(\sin\left(\delta x_{1}\right)-\delta x_{1})\end{bmatrix}\,,\end{split}\] (37)

where \(l=1\), \(g=9.8,\) and \(\mu=0.01\) (as in [13]). In this example, \(\mathbf{B}_{2}=\mathbf{1}_{2_{2}}\), \(\mathbf{C}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1_{3_{1}}&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{D}_{1}=\mathbf{0}.\) Since the nonlinearity is independent of \(\delta u\), we do not necessarily need to constrain the control input. However, performing the iterations in Algorithm 3.3.1 to reduce \(\bar{\sigma}(\overline{\mathbf{KW}})\) in turn reduces the control effort required, and we let these iterations continue for \(n_{\text{max}}=20\). In this setup, the maximum certified radius is \(\alpha=\sqrt{2},\) along with the controller \(\mathbf{K}=$-13.4283$~\,{-}~$13.5242$\,.](33)\) This controller is therefore able to drive the pendulum to its upright position from an initial displacement of approximately \(81\) degrees. The simulation results of the system (33) with this controller are depicted in Fig. 2 where, similar to Example-1, the vector field indicates that the closed-loop system can be driven to the equilibrium from a much larger region than the certified region $\mathbb{X}_{c}$. Indeed, there appears to be a stable manifold with the vector field converging to it (see Fig. 2). Also in Fig. 2, the red square denotes the local region certified in [13]. In comparison, the proposed controller is able to certify a much larger region. This improvement was achieved, in part, by utilizing the knowledge of the nominal LTI system whereas, the controller in [13] is purely data-driven. This example thus demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method over a purely data-driven framework, given the nominal LTI system is known.

## V Conclusions and Future Work

We presented an iterative method of local stabilization for nonlinear systems using sampled I/O data. Our approach uses I/O data to derive local norm bounds and synthesizes a robust state-feedback controller that is guaranteed to stabilize the system within the sampling region for the set of nonlinearities satisfying the norm bounds. The iterative steps require solving SDPs which can be done efficiently using freely available solvers. One of the numerical examples highlighted the reduced conservatism in our proposed synthesis method compared to a purely data-driven approach. Our future efforts will involve introducing parametric uncertainties and exogenous signals into the proposed framework. Also, we will investigate other ways to characterize I/O behavior of the nonlinearities (e.g., weighted 2-norm bounds) and extend our formulation to the output-feedback case.
